concepts.name: Crown rule after 1857: the royal proclamation, paramountcy and discrimination
concepts.description: How the British Crown took direct charge of India in 1858, what the royal proclamation promised the princes and the 'natives', how each of those promises was broken in practice, and the racial discrimination and repressive laws Indians lived under afterwards.
concepts.idea: In 1858 the ruler of India changed from a trading company to the British Crown, and the language of rule became generous, but the control and the exploitation did not change at all.
concepts.rule: From 1858 British India was governed in the Queen's name by the Secretary of State for India in London and the Viceroy, also called Governor General, in India. The royal proclamation promised to respect the rights, dignity and honour of some 560 native Princes, who would rule under British supremacy called paramountcy, and promised the 'natives' care equal to other subjects and no imposition of Christianity. None of these assurances were respected in practice: Residents and Political Agents interfered in the princely states, missionary activity continued with state support, heavy land taxes brought famines, and Indians were treated as an inferior race in pay, in the courts and in public places.
concepts.example: In 1878 the Arms Act stopped Indians from keeping arms while allowing the British to do so, and the Vernacular Press Act censored the Indian-language press -- both passed twenty years after the Crown promised Indians would be cared for like all other subjects.

Residents and Political Agents interfered so much in the princely states that their autonomy became symbolic; missionary work continued with land concessions and official encouragement; and heavy taxes, famines and unequal treatment went on as before. The ruler's name changed from the Company to the Crown, but the control and the exploitation did not.

questions.q: The chapter gives several examples of Indians being treated as inferior after 1858. Analyse what these examples have in common.
questions.a: Sample: Indians in the army, civil services and universities were paid less than British employees in the same posts; juries usually had a British majority and were lenient towards crimes by Europeans against 'natives'; and Indians could not mix with Europeans in clubs, trains and certain parts of cities. Behind all of them lay the belief that Indians belonged to 'inferior races' and that the white race was destined to dominate the world. What they share is that the inequality was not private prejudice but was built into pay scales, courts and public rules -- it was official.
s: Gives at least two of the chapter's examples, such as unequal pay, British-majority juries or exclusion from public spaces

questions.q: The chapter says the proclamation promised no attempt to impose Christianity, and also says missionary activity continued with support. Analyse whether these two statements contradict each other.
questions.a: Sample: The proclamation's promise was narrow -- it said no attempt would be made to impose Christianity on anyone. What the chapter then describes is not forced conversion but assistance: urban land granted on concession, and open encouragement from British high officials. Strictly read, assisting missionaries is not the same as imposing a religion, so the two statements do not contradict each other on the letter of the promise. But the promise was clearly meant to reassure Indians that the state would stay out of religion, and a state that funds one religion's missionaries has not stayed out of it. So the promise was kept in its wording and broken in its spirit.
s: States the exact promise made in the proclamation
States what actually happened: indirect state support and open official encouragement
Distinguishes not forcing conversion from actively assisting missionaries
Reaches a judgement: kept in the letter, broken in the spirit

questions.q: The Arms Act and the Vernacular Press Act were both passed in 1878. Evaluate what this pairing suggests about what the colonial government feared.
questions.a: Sample: The Arms Act kept weapons out of Indian hands while leaving them in British ones, and the Vernacular Press Act regulated and censored newspapers printed in Indian languages. One controls the means of armed resistance; the other controls the spread of ideas among people who do not read English. Passing them in the same year suggests the government feared not one danger but two -- that Indians might take up arms, and that Indian-language newspapers might build the shared opinion that makes such action possible. The second fear is the more revealing, because it admits that words were treated as dangerous as weapons.
s: States accurately what each of the two Acts did
Identifies the two things being controlled: weapons and the spread of ideas in Indian languages
Reaches a judgement about what the pairing reveals of British fears

concepts.name: Reform movements and the cultural awakening
concepts.description: The reform movements that challenged social practices from within Indian society, and the two cultural currents the chapter singles out -- Bankim's Bande Mataram and Swami Vivekananda's call to inner strength -- which fed the rise of nationalist feeling.
concepts.idea: Before the political struggle grew strong, reformers were changing Indian society from inside it, and writers and teachers were giving Indians back their confidence in their own civilisation.
concepts.rule: The reform movements took note of European models while challenging the lack of formal education, child marriage, the degraded status of widows and caste-based discrimination. Brahmo Samaj was founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy in 1828 at Calcutta, Arya Samaj by Swami Dayananda Saraswati in 1875 at Bombay, and the Shuddhi Movement by Arya Samaj leaders late in the 19th century. Alongside them, Bankim's poem Bande Mataram and Swami Vivekananda's teaching supplied the cultural pride and self-confidence on which nationalism was later built.
concepts.example: The poem Bande Mataram was composed in 1875, printed in the novel Anandamath in 1882, set to music and sung by Rabindranath Tagore at the 1896 Congress session, became a rallying cry in 1905, and was adopted as India's National Song in 1950.

concepts.name: The 1905 Partition of Bengal, Swadeshi and boycott

concepts.idea: A division meant to weaken Bengal produced instead the first mass programme of the freedom struggle, because people answered a political split with economic self-reliance.
concepts.rule: George Curzon, then viceroy, announced the partition of the Bengal presidency in 1905. concepts.idea: Between 1906 and 1907 the demand changed from reform to Swaraj, and the Congress split over whether to make that demand at all.
concepts.rule: In 1906 Bipin Chandra Pal launched the English daily Bande Mataram, which Aurobindo Ghose soon took charge of; it added National Education to Swadeshi and boycott and spelt out a doctrine of passive resistance. In December 1906 the Congress session at Calcutta, with Dadabhai Naoroji as president, declared Swaraj, Swadeshi, boycott and National Education to be the Congress's objective, but left 'Swaraj' undefined. The same December the All-India Muslim League was founded at Dhaka. At Surat in December 1907 the Moderates tried to step back from the Calcutta resolutions, and the Nationalists walked out to hold their own session.
concepts.example: The Nationalists were labelled 'Extremists' or 'Radicals' by the Moderates and the British, but called themselves simply Nationalists, seeing nothing extreme in wanting an independent Indian nation.

questions.q: Apply the chapter's account to explain why the British authorities were alarmed by the Calcutta resolution of 1906 and what they did about it.
questions.a: Sample: Until then the Congress had asked for dialogue, reform and a share in governance, all of which left British rule in place. The Calcutta session declared Swaraj an objective, and since Swaraj was undefined it could mean full independence -- so the demand was no longer about the terms of British rule but about whether it should continue. The authorities did not attack the Congress directly; they exerted pressure on some of the moderate Congress leaders. The effect showed at Surat a year later, where those Moderates tried to step back from the Calcutta resolutions, and the Congress split.
s: Explains why the demand for Swaraj was different from earlier Congress demands
States that the authorities exerted pressure on some moderate Congress leaders

questions.q: Analyse what the Moderates and the Nationalists disagreed about at Surat, given that both wanted a better position for India.
questions.a: Sample: They agreed that India's position had to improve and disagreed about how far and how fast. The Moderates wanted to return to the old requests -- minor administrative concessions and a gradual shift to self-government within the British Empire -- which meant accepting British rule as the setting for improvement. The Nationalists, led by Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai and Aurobindo Ghose, would settle for nothing less than independence, which meant treating British rule as the problem itself. Because one side was negotiating within the empire and the other was trying to end it, no single resolution could carry both, and when Tilak was prevented from speaking the session collapsed into chaos and the Nationalists walked out.
s: States the Moderate position: minor concessions and gradual self-government within the British Empire
States the Nationalist position: nothing less than independence
Explains why the disagreement could not be contained in one session, referring to the walkout

questions.q: December 1906 saw both the Congress declare Swaraj at Calcutta and the All-India Muslim League founded at Dhaka. Analyse how this chapter connects the two events.
questions.a: Sample: The chapter puts them in the same month deliberately. The Swadeshi movement had spread the ideal of liberation from colonial rule, and the Calcutta session turned that into the Congress's declared objective. But the same growth made some Muslim leaders more anxious, not less: their concerns had been rising ever since the Congress was formed, they distrusted it, and they feared Muslims would not be adequately represented in a largely Hindu-dominated body. So the League was founded to defend Muslim political interests. The chapter is careful to add that it initially represented a limited segment, primarily the elite, and that quite a few Muslims had opposed the partition of Bengal -- and then notes that a few decades later this division would contribute to the emergence of the Two-Nation Idea.
s: States what the Calcutta session declared and the context of the spreading Swadeshi movement
States why the League was founded, including the fear of inadequate representation
Notes the chapter's qualification that the League initially represented mainly the elite, or that many Muslims had opposed the partition
Notes the chapter's forward link to the emergence of the Two-Nation Idea decades later

questions.q: Evaluate the decision of the Calcutta session to declare Swaraj without defining it.
questions.a: Sample: Leaving it undefined had a real advantage. Swaraj could then mean self-rule within the British Empire to a Moderate and full independence to a Nationalist, so both could support the same resolution and the Congress could declare a bold objective while staying one body. The cost appeared within a year. Because nobody had settled what had been agreed, the Moderates could try at Surat to step back from it, the Nationalists could insist it meant independence, and the Congress split instead of holding together. So the vagueness bought unity at the moment of the declaration and lost it at the first test -- which suggests it postponed the argument rather than solving it.
s: States the advantage: a word broad enough for both Moderates and Nationalists to accept
States the cost, using the Surat split as the evidence
Reaches a judgement on whether the vagueness was worth it

questions.q: Compose a short exchange, of two or three lines each, between a Moderate and a Nationalist delegate meeting outside the Surat session in December 1907. Keep both voices to the positions this chapter records.
questions.a: Sample: Moderate: 'We have gained a hearing in thirty years by patience and by reason. Ask for a gradual self-government within the Empire and you may get it; shout for Swaraj and they will close even the door we have opened.' Nationalist: 'A door they may close at will was never open. We were promised in 1858 that we would be treated as their other subjects, and you saw what that was worth. Swaraj is not extreme -- it is only the ordinary condition of every nation that governs itself, and we shall not call it by a smaller name to make them comfortable.'
s: Gives the Moderate the position of gradual self-government within the Empire and minor concessions
Gives the Nationalist the demand for nothing less than independence and the rejection of the 'extreme' label
Keeps both voices to what the chapter records and invents no new demand or event

concepts.name: The revolutionaries: Alipore, the Cellular Jail, Ghadar and the German Plot
concepts.description: The Nationalist and revolutionary press, the Khudiram Bose attempt and the Alipore Bomb trial, Tilak's sedition trial, the individual attacks on British officials, the Ghadar Movement, the Cellular Jail, and Bagha Jatin's German Plot.
concepts.idea: Alongside the Congress there ran a second struggle, of newspapers that preached revolt and of very young people who took up arms, and the state answered it with sedition trials and the Cellular Jail.
concepts.rule: From the late 19th century newspapers in English and Indian languages questioned colonial policies: Kesari and Bande Mataram among the Nationalist papers, Voice of India and The Bengalee among the moderate ones, and Yugantar, which preached open revolt. Revolutionary action followed -- the attempt on Kingsford in 1908 and the year-long Alipore Bomb trial, attacks on officials between 1909 and 1912, the Ghadar Movement of 1914-15 and the German Plot of 1915. Those caught were hanged, given long terms, or sent to the Cellular Jail in the Andaman Islands.
concepts.example: Khudiram Bose was just 18 when he was hanged; Kartar Singh Sarabha was 19 and Anant Kanhere 18 -- the chapter keeps giving these ages.

questions.q: Explain why the Cellular Jail became a symbol of ultimate sacrifice in India's struggle for freedom.
questions.a: It was a huge colonial prison used to exile and isolate revolutionaries far from the mainland, and it was designed specifically for solitary confinement in order to break the spirit of freedom fighters. Prisoners faced horrific conditions, including extreme physical labour such as extracting oil by hand, and brutal punishment for the slightest disobedience. Many died, some lost their sanity, and those who tried to escape were hanged.

questions.q: Explain what the Ghadar Movement of 1914-15 tried to do, and why it failed.
questions.a: It was a daring attempt by Indian revolutionaries to trigger a pan-Indian mutiny within the British Indian Army during World War I, and in India men such as Rash Behari Bose, Sachindra Nath Sanyal and Kartar Singh Sarabha tried to get the army infiltrated. It failed because the British intelligence network uncovered the plot, which led to widespread arrests, imprisonments in the Cellular Jail and several executions.
s: States the aim: to trigger a mutiny within the British Indian Army during World War I

questions.q: Describe the German Plot and what happened at Balasore on 9 September 1915.
questions.a: The German Plot was a plan by Jatin Mukherjee, nicknamed Bagha Jatin because he had once wrestled a tiger with his bare hands, working with Rash Behari Bose, to receive a massive shipment of German arms and ammunition by ship and use it to start an armed insurrection while the British were occupied with World War I. The authorities learnt of the plan, forcing the group to hide in the jungles of Balasore, where on 9 September 1915 they were surrounded by a large contingent of British police and fought a 75-minute gunbattle from behind an anthill; Jatin, severely wounded, died the next day.
s: Explains the plot: Bagha Jatin receiving a shipment of German arms to start an insurrection during World War I
Describes the Balasore gunbattle and Bagha Jatin's death the next day

questions.q: Apply the chapter's account to explain why the colonial authorities moved against the Nationalist press at the same time as the revolutionaries.
questions.a: Sample: The two were connected in fact, not only in the government's mind. Yugantar preached open revolt and was run by a group of revolutionaries led by Barindra and associated with the Anushilan Samiti -- the same circle from which Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki came. So when the Alipore arrests were made, suppressing Bande Mataram and jailing Nationalist leaders followed naturally: the papers supplied the arguments and the reputation that made the actions popular. Tilak was prosecuted for sedition over his articles in Kesari rather than for anything he had done. The government had concluded that the writing was the more dangerous half.
s: Notes the actual link between Yugantar, the Anushilan Samiti and the Alipore accused
Notes the suppression of Bande Mataram during the trial and the jailing of Nationalist leaders
Notes that Tilak was prosecuted over his articles rather than over an action

questions.q: The chapter says the attacks on British officials 'rattled the colonial government, but, at the same time, hardened its resolve to rule with an iron hand'. Analyse this double effect using the events of 1908 to 1915.
questions.a: Sample: The rattling is easy to see. Bombs reached a Viceroy's carriage at Ahmedabad, a district magistrate was shot in a Nashik theatre, a district collector was shot at a railway station near Tirunelveli, and a bomb injured Viceroy Hardinge in Delhi itself -- no official anywhere was safe, and the attacks invariably met with strong popular approval. But every incident was answered with more force, not less: hangings soon after Nashik, the year-long Alipore trial, suppression of the Nationalist press, sedition sentences for Tilak, and mass imprisonment in the Cellular Jail after the Ghadar plot was uncovered. Attacks that proved the government vulnerable also gave it the justification it needed for harsher rule.
s: Gives at least two of the attacks as evidence that the government was rattled
Gives at least two of the repressive responses
Explains the double effect: the attacks both alarmed the government and justified harsher rule

questions.q: The chapter keeps recording the ages of the revolutionaries it names. Analyse what this repeated detail is doing in the account.
questions.a: Sample: Khudiram Bose was 18 when hanged, Anant Kanhere was 18, Kartar Singh Sarabha was 19, and Birsa Munda died at 24. Giving the age turns each of them from a name in a list into someone the reader's own age or a little older, which is a different kind of fact from a date. It also measures the cost: these were not experienced politicians who had lived their lives but people who lost almost all of theirs. And it explains the public reaction the chapter records, such as crowds throwing flowers on Khudiram's body as his funeral procession went through Calcutta, and the report that he was calm and smiling at the end. The ages are how the chapter conveys sacrifice without having to describe it.
s: Cites at least two of the ages the chapter gives
Explains the effect of making the figures close to the reader in age
Connects the ages to the measure of what was sacrificed
Connects them to the popular reaction the chapter records, such as the response to Khudiram's death

questions.q: The chapter says the Ghadar mutiny failed but 'laid the groundwork for future revolutionary efforts'. Evaluate that judgement.
questions.a: Sample: By its own aim it failed completely. The pan-Indian mutiny never happened, British intelligence uncovered the plot, and it cost the lives of leaders including Kartar Singh Sarabha at 19 and Vishnu Ganesh Pingle, with many others imprisoned in the Cellular Jail. Yet the chapter's claim holds up in the events that follow. Rash Behari Bose escaped to Japan and there laid the foundation of the Indian National Army; Bagha Jatin worked with him on the German Plot within months; and much later Udham Singh, who killed O'Dwyer, was a member of the Ghadar Party. A failed plan that supplies people, methods and an example to the next attempt has done something, even though it did not do what it set out to do.
s: States the respects in which it plainly failed, with the cost in lives
Gives evidence from later events, such as Rash Behari Bose and the Indian National Army
Reaches a judgement on whether the chapter's claim is justified

questions.q: Write a short newspaper paragraph, of about four sentences, as a Calcutta paper might have reported the verdict of the Alipore Bomb trial. Report only what this chapter records.
questions.a: Sample: 'The Alipore Bomb trial, which has held the attention of the whole country for a year, closed yesterday. Mr Aurobindo Ghose, whom the authorities had called the most dangerous man they have to deal with at present, has been acquitted, ably defended throughout by his friend Mr Chittaranjan Das. His brother Barindra and one other accused were sentenced to death, a sentence we are informed may yet be commuted on appeal to transportation for life to the Cellular Jail. Of the remainder, most received long terms of imprisonment and a few were acquitted.'
s: Reports Aurobindo's acquittal and names Chittaranjan Das as his defender
Reports the death sentences on Barindra and another, and the commutation on appeal
Reports the long terms for most others and adds nothing the chapter does not state

concepts.name: Home Rule, Gandhi's satyagraha, Non-Cooperation and Jallianwala Bagh
concepts.description: Tilak's three tasks and the Lucknow Pact, the Home Rule Movement, Gandhi's method of satyagraha and his early campaigns, the Rowlatt Act and the launch of the Non-Cooperation Movement, and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and its aftermath.
concepts.idea: Between 1914 and 1920 the struggle changed shape: the two wings of the Congress came back together, a new method arrived with Gandhi, and one massacre destroyed whatever trust in British rule remained.
concepts.rule: Satyagraha means insistence on truth, and is based on passive resistance, nonviolence or ahimsa, and the acceptance of suffering in the quest for truth. Gandhi conceived it in South Africa, returned to India in 1915 on Gokhale's advice, and applied it to local grievances before turning it against the Rowlatt Act of 1919, which let the police detain anyone without trial. The Non-Cooperation Movement that followed asked Indians to boycott foreign goods, schools and courts, and Gandhi promised Swaraj within a year if people kept strictly to nonviolence.
concepts.example: Gandhi spinning khadi was not only about making cloth: it was a symbol of Swadeshi, work for millions of poor villagers, and a direct challenge to British textile imports.

questions.q: Apply this chapter's account to explain why the end of World War I brought anger rather than relief in India.
questions.a: Sample: The war had been fought with Indian help but ended with no freedom for Indians. During it the colonial government had exported food to feed soldiers, which caused food shortages at home, and massive defence spending drove up the price of everything else. Then, instead of a reward, came the Rowlatt Act of 1919, which let the police detain anyone without trial and effectively curtailed civil liberties altogether. Hardship endured for a distant war, followed by a new law taking away what freedom remained, is why the peace brought protest rather than celebration.
s: States the wartime hardships: food exported causing shortages, and rising commodity prices
States that the war's end brought no freedom to Indians
States the Rowlatt Act of 1919 and what it allowed

questions.q: Assertion (A): Gandhi's Non-Cooperation Movement asked Indians to actively participate in British-run schools and courts. Reason (R): The Simon Commission of 1927 came without a single Indian member and was met with the slogan 'Simon Go Back'. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, R is true
o: A is false, R is true
A is true, R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: Analyse how the Home Rule demand of 1916 differed from what the Nationalists had demanded a decade earlier, and why it was nonetheless refused.
questions.a: Sample: The Nationalists of the previous decade had wanted nothing less than full independence. The Home Rule Movement, launched by Tilak with Annie Besant, asked only for self-government within the British Empire -- a measure of real internal autonomy, which was perceived as a practical first step rather than the final goal. It was a deliberately smaller demand, made by a Tilak whose health had deteriorated in jail and in a country where the militant atmosphere of the previous decade had faded. Yet the British government was not ready to concede even this. That refusal is what mattered: if the modest demand was also impossible, there was nothing left to negotiate, and the struggle moved instead towards mass political mobilisation.
s: States the earlier Nationalist demand for full independence
States the Home Rule demand of self-government within the British Empire as a practical first step
Notes the British refusal and what followed from it

questions.q: Analyse why the chapter says Jallianwala Bagh 'permanently scarred public trust in the British government', drawing on what happened both during and after the massacre.
questions.a: Sample: What happened in the garden was bad enough: Dyer sealed the main exit before firing, about 1,650 rounds were poured into an unarmed crowd for some ten minutes, the troops aimed deliberately at the thickest parts of it and at those fleeing, and people were trampled or leapt into a well. But the chapter puts as much weight on what came afterwards. Dyer proudly defended his action before a British-dominated inquiry committee, which condemned it yet recommended no penal action, and he was only removed from India after a general outcry. O'Dwyer, who had ruthlessly suppressed rights in Punjab, defended him. And to this day the British government has not apologised, calling it only a 'deeply shameful event'. A massacre might be blamed on one officer; a system that then declines to punish him is harder to trust, which is why the chapter says Indians of all backgrounds were united in their resolve to attain freedom.
s: Describes what Dyer's troops did, using detail such as the sealed exit, the rounds fired or the deliberate aiming
Describes the inquiry: condemnation without penal action, and Dyer removed only after a general outcry
Notes the absence of an apology to this day, or O'Dwyer's defence of Dyer
Draws the conclusion about why trust in the government, and not only in one officer, was destroyed

questions.q: Gandhi promised Swaraj within a year if people adhered strictly to nonviolence. Evaluate what such a promise would have gained and risked.
questions.a: Sample: The gain is clear from what followed: the movement soon drew mass participation across India, and a promise with a date and a condition gives ordinary people a reason to act now rather than wait for leaders to negotiate. It also made nonviolence everyone's responsibility, since the promise was conditional on it. The risk is equally clear. A deadline can be missed, and Swaraj did not arrive within a year, which leaves supporters disappointed and opponents able to say the method had been tested and failed. The condition also placed the whole movement at the mercy of any one crowd that lost its discipline -- which is exactly what happened at Chauri Chaura.
s: States the gain: mass participation and a clear, immediate reason for ordinary people to act
States the risk of a deadline that is missed, or of resting everything on universal nonviolence
Reaches a judgement, supported by what actually followed

questions.q: Draft the text of a short poster, of about four lines, calling people to join the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920. Include only the actions this chapter says the movement asked for.
questions.a: Sample: 'Countrymen -- do not cooperate with a government that jails without trial. Leave the foreign goods on the shelf, take your children out of their schools and your disputes out of their courts. Wear only what Indian hands have spun and woven. Keep strictly to nonviolence, and Mahatma Gandhi has promised us Swaraj within the year.'
s: Calls for the boycott of foreign goods, and of schools or courts
Includes the insistence on strict nonviolence
Includes the promise of Swaraj within a year and adds no action the chapter does not record

concepts.name: Khilafat, Chauri Chaura, the Simon Commission and Civil Disobedience
concepts.description: The Khilafat Movement and its aftermath, the calling off of Non-Cooperation after Chauri Chaura, the Simon Commission and the death of Lala Lajpat Rai, the HSRA revolutionaries, and the road from Purna Swaraj through the Salt March to the Gandhi-Irwin Pact and the Poona Pact.
concepts.idea: Through the 1920s and early 1930s the movement kept alternating between mass campaigns that were called off and revolutionary actions that were punished, while the demand itself hardened from Dominion status into complete independence.
concepts.rule: The Khilafat Movement, launched in 1919 to preserve the Caliph's religious authority, was allied with the Congress in 1920 and merged with Non-Cooperation. Gandhi called Non-Cooperation off after Chauri Chaura in February 1922. The Simon Commission of 1927 came without a single Indian member and was met with 'Simon Go Back'. In December 1929 the Lahore session demanded Purna Swaraj, and Gandhi launched Civil Disobedience with the Salt March of March-April 1930; the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 1931 suspended it.
concepts.example: Bhagat Singh and an associate dropped two low-intensity bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly where there were no victims, because the intention was only 'to make the deaf hear'.

questions.q: Explain how the Khilafat Movement came to an end and what the chapter says historians have debated about it.
questions.a: It died a natural death when Mustafa Kemal abolished the Turkish sultanate in 1922 and the Caliphate itself in 1924, so there was no longer a Caliph whose authority could be preserved. Historians have debated its aftermath: while it temporarily united Hindus and Muslims, it also reinforced the sense of separateness among Indian Muslims and encouraged more radical Muslim leaders to come up with fresh demands. In fact the following years saw quite a few Hindu-Muslim riots in several parts of the country.

questions.q: What was 'Dominion status' as the Motilal Nehru report of 1928 sought it, and why did younger leaders turn away from it?
questions.a: Dominion status meant total internal autonomy, somewhat like the earlier Home Rule, but Britain would still control India's military and foreign policy and the British king or queen would remain the official head of state; Canada and Australia already had this status. Younger leaders such as Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose turned away from it because of growing popular anger and the realisation that Britain was not ready to grant India even that, so they felt it was time for the more radical demand of Purna Swaraj.
s: Defines Dominion status: total internal autonomy, with Britain keeping military and foreign policy and the Crown as head of state

questions.q: Describe the Salt March and explain why Gandhi chose the salt law to break.
questions.a: In March and April 1930 Gandhi led a 380-km march to Dandi, a coastal village in southern Gujarat, where he symbolically collected some salt; the march is also known as the Dandi March. He chose salt because the colonial government held a monopoly on salt production and charged a high tax for it, so breaking the colonial salt law was an appropriate symbol in the fight against colonial rule.
s: Describes the march: 380 km to Dandi in southern Gujarat in March-April 1930, ending in collecting salt
Explains the choice: the government monopoly on salt production and the high tax made it an apt symbol

questions.q: Apply the chapter's account to explain Gandhi's decision after Chauri Chaura and why so many in the Congress disagreed with it.
questions.a: Sample: Gandhi had launched Non-Cooperation on the condition that people adhere strictly to nonviolence, and had promised Swaraj within a year on that basis. At Chauri Chaura protesters killed policemen by setting a station on fire, which he viewed as 'inhuman conduct' -- so by his own terms the movement had failed its condition and he abruptly called it off. Many disagreed, including Motilal Nehru, Jawaharlal Nehru, Chittaranjan Das and Subhas Chandra Bose, because the movement had drawn mass participation across the whole country and one incident was being allowed to end it. Motilal Nehru and Chittaranjan Das went on to create the Swaraj Party to attempt a different strategy.
s: States the condition of strict nonviolence on which the movement rested
States what happened at Chauri Chaura and Gandhi's judgement of it as 'inhuman conduct'
Names those who disapproved and what Motilal Nehru and Chittaranjan Das did next

questions.q: Analyse what was striking about women's participation in the Civil Disobedience Movement, using the evidence the chapter gives.
questions.a: Sample: Large numbers of women broke the salt law, joined processions and picketed liquor shops and shops selling foreign cloth. What makes it striking is where they came from: a British report noted that thousands of women, many of good family and high educational attainments, suddenly emerged from the seclusion of their homes and in some cases actually from purdah in order to join Congress demonstrations. That the observation comes from a British official report matters, because it is the opponent recording the change. And there were women already at the head of the movement -- Sarojini Naidu, a noted poet and powerful orator, had been the first Indian woman president of the Congress in 1925, and was arrested and imprisoned several times.
s: Names at least two forms of participation: breaking the salt law, processions, picketing
Uses the British report's observation about women emerging from seclusion and from purdah
Uses Sarojini Naidu as evidence of women's leadership, noting her 1925 presidency

questions.q: Analyse the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 1931: what each side gave, what it achieved, and why younger Congress leaders criticised it.
questions.a: Sample: The government released political prisoners who had not been involved in violence and allowed a limited private manufacture of salt. In return the Congress suspended civil disobedience and agreed to take part in a Round Table Conference in London. Its real achievement was in status rather than substance: the chapter calls it the first formal negotiation between the British government and the Congress as equals, which is not nothing after decades of being ignored. But the Conference failed to produce a breakthrough, and younger leaders criticised the pact because it did not guarantee Purna Swaraj -- the Congress had given up an active mass movement in exchange for talks and some prisoners. What followed supports them: when Gandhi tried to resume the movement the British answered with massive arrests, public enthusiasm was missing, and he withdrew it in 1934.
s: States what the government conceded: release of prisoners not involved in violence, limited private salt manufacture
States what the Congress conceded: suspending civil disobedience and attending the Round Table Conference
Notes the achievement of a first formal negotiation as equals, and that the Conference failed
States the criticism that it did not guarantee Purna Swaraj, supported by what happened afterwards

questions.q: Gandhi and Ambedkar disagreed about separate electorates for the Depressed Classes. Evaluate the compromise they reached.
questions.a: Sample: Both wanted the same thing -- an end to the discrimination suffered by those rejected by the caste system -- and disagreed about the means. Ambedkar, who had himself suffered that discrimination, held that separate electorates were the only way to ensure their political voice. Gandhi feared this would permanently divide Hindu society and began a fast unto death against it. The Poona Pact settled it by increasing the number of reserved seats for the Depressed Classes in the legislatures instead of creating separate electorates. It gave each side something real: Ambedkar got guaranteed representation, Gandhi avoided a separate electorate. But it was reached under a fast unto death, which is a hard pressure to argue against, and the reserved seats were chosen by all voters rather than by the group itself -- so it answered the question of numbers more convincingly than the question of voice.
s: States Ambedkar's position and the reason behind it
States Gandhi's objection and the fast unto death
States the Poona Pact terms and reaches a judgement about the compromise

questions.q: Write a short diary entry, of about four sentences, by a soldier of the Royal Garhwal Rifles at Peshawar on 23 April 1930, explaining the choice his platoon made. Use only what this chapter records.
questions.a: Sample: 'They had gathered in the Qissa Khwani Bazaar to protest peacefully at the arrest of Abdul Ghaffar Khan, who has never asked anyone to lift a hand in anger. The order came to fire, and the armoured cars were already among them; hundreds were killed before us. Our two platoons would not do it, for these were our own countrymen and unarmed. We are told what waits for us now, and we have chosen the jail.'
s: Names the Qissa Khwani Bazaar protest and that it followed the arrest of Abdul Ghaffar Khan
Refers accurately to the firing on the unarmed crowd
States the platoons' refusal to fire and their choosing jail over hurting fellow Indians

concepts.name: Separate nations, World War II, the INA, Quit India and Partition
concepts.description: The idea of separate nations, India's part in World War II, Subhas Chandra Bose and the Indian National Army, the Cripps Mission and the Quit India Movement, and the events of 1946-47 that ended in Partition and Independence.
concepts.idea: The last decade of the struggle brought independence and Partition together, so that the chapter's closing judgement is of a legacy of both triumph and tragedy.
concepts.rule: World War II strained India enormously, and the war years produced both the Quit India Movement of 1942 and Subhas Chandra Bose's Indian National Army. After the war Britain was exhausted, decolonisation had begun and the mutinies of 1946 showed the British they could no longer rely on the Indian military. The Cabinet Mission ended in deadlock, Direct Action Day was followed by brutal communal violence, and in 1947 Mountbatten had Cyril Radcliffe draw the Radcliffe Line in five weeks, splitting Punjab and Bengal.
concepts.example: The partition plan was widely opposed even by the Indian National Congress, and the chapter says there was no national consensus and that whether it was the only way forward has been debated ever since.

questions.q: Explain how Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel dealt with the princely states and why he came to be called the Iron Man of India.
questions.a: When the British announced their departure, the over 560 princely states were given the option to join either India or Pakistan and were also technically free to remain independent, which the chapter calls a classic colonial step to destroy the integrity of India. Patel had always believed the states were an integral part of India, and both before and after Independence he used a mix of persuasion and firmness to integrate them; while most joined peacefully, he used military action as a last resort for the few that refused or delayed merger. Because his efforts ensured that modern India became a geographically unified nation, he came to be known as the Iron Man of India.
s: States the choice the princely states were given and that the chapter treats it as a move against India's integrity
States Patel's method of persuasion and firmness, with military action as a last resort, and the unified nation that resulted

questions.q: Trace Subhas Chandra Bose's journey after escaping India, and say what he formed in 1943.
questions.a: Escaping house arrest in India in early 1941, he travelled through Afghanistan and Russia to reach Germany, where he spent almost two years seeking support from the anti-British forces. Deciding he stood a better chance with Japan, he travelled to Indonesia, Japan and finally Singapore in 1943, where he formed the Indian National Army from Indian prisoners of war and volunteers and declared the formation of the Azad Hind, or free India, government.
s: Traces the route: escape in early 1941, through Afghanistan and Russia to Germany, then to Indonesia, Japan and Singapore in 1943
States that he formed the Indian National Army from prisoners of war and volunteers and declared the Azad Hind government

questions.q: Apply the chapter's account to explain why most Indian leaders rejected the Cripps Mission of 1942.
questions.a: Sample: Churchill sent Stafford Cripps under pressure to secure India's support during the war, and the offer was dominion status -- not independence -- and only once the war was over. It also carried a provision that provinces could opt out of the post-war India, which meant the offer contained the seed of a partition. A few leaders such as C. Rajagopalachari favoured accepting for tactical reasons, but most, including Gandhi, found the assurances in the proposal insufficient and ended up rejecting it. A promise of something less than freedom, deferred to an unknown date and conditional on cooperation now, was not worth the cooperation it asked for -- and within months Gandhi launched Quit India instead.
s: States what the offer was: dominion status once the war was over, with provinces able to opt out
Notes that C. Rajagopalachari favoured acceptance while most, including Gandhi, found the assurances insufficient
Explains why the offer was judged not worth accepting

questions.q: Analyse the causes of Partition as this chapter sets them out.
questions.a: Sample: The chapter puts several causes side by side rather than naming one. It says the British had for decades encouraged Hindu Muslim differences to grow. It says the partition resulted from disagreements between the two communities, or rather small sections of them. It records the effect of Direct Action Day, after which the violence in Calcutta created a deep sense of fear that made peaceful coexistence seem impossible and partition unavoidable. And it is careful to add what is often forgotten: the partition plan was widely opposed even by the Indian National Congress, and there was no national consensus for it. The chapter then leaves the question open, saying that whether it was the only way forward has been debated ever since.
s: Notes that the British had for decades encouraged Hindu Muslim differences to grow
Notes the disagreements between the communities and the fear created after Direct Action Day
Notes that the plan was widely opposed even by the Congress, with no national consensus, and that the chapter leaves the question open

questions.q: The chapter says the earlier view of why Britain left India has given way to another. Analyse both views and what caused the change.
questions.a: Sample: The earlier view was that Britain's exit was mostly thanks to Gandhi, his doctrine of nonviolence and the Congress's policies -- a single movement led by one man and one party. The chapter says this has given way to a recognition that multiple other factors were also at work: the popular uprisings, the numerous attempts by revolutionaries, and the mutinies in the Royal Indian Air Force and the Royal Indian Navy, together with Britain's diminished status after World War II and the worldwide trend towards decolonisation. What forces the change is the evidence the chapter has been assembling all along -- the Kukas, Birsa Munda, the Ghadar Movement, the INA, the mutinies -- none of which belongs to the Gandhian story, and the plain fact that the age of empires was ending everywhere at once. The second view does not take Gandhi out of the account; it stops treating him as the whole of it.
s: States the earlier view accurately
States the factors the later view adds, naming at least three
Explains what supports the change of view, using evidence from the chapter
Notes that the later view supplements rather than replaces the role of Gandhi and the Congress

questions.q: The Quit India Movement was brutally suppressed and did not force the British out in 1942. Evaluate whether it should nonetheless be counted a success.
questions.a: Sample: By its stated demand it failed: the British did not leave at once, virtually the entire Congress leadership was arrested, and the movement was brutally suppressed with many deaths and numerous arrests. But the test of a mass movement is also what it proves. With its leaders in jail the movement continued anyway -- workers struck, students left schools, government buildings were attacked and telegraph poles uprooted, and Lohia and Jayaprakash Narayan kept an underground network going. The Viceroy himself called it by far the most serious rebellion since 1857, which is the opponent's own measure of it.
